# Foundations

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/01-foundations.yml` and not yet reviewed by a second
reader.
:::

One gene, one protein was always an approximation, and it stopped being a useful
one as soon as transcripts could be counted directly. The harder question that
replaced it is which of a gene's several transcripts matter, and why.

Three processes generate those transcripts: exons spliced in different
combinations, transcription starting in different places, and polyadenylation
ending the molecule in different places. Each of the three affects at least half
of human protein-coding genes [@carrion2023alternativetranscripts]. So isoform
is not a synonym for splice variant, and this book keeps the two terms apart.

## The machine that removes an intron {#sec-mechanism}

Splicing is done by an assembly rather than by an enzyme. Five small nuclear
ribonucleoproteins, U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6, work together with hundreds of
further proteins. The complex is built fresh on every pre-mRNA, through an
ordered series of intermediates named E, A, B and C, and only the E complex
forms without ATP [@borao2021earlyspliceosome].

The two ends of an intron are recognised by different machinery, in a definite
order. U1 engages the 5' splice site, while SF1 and U2AF recognise the 3' splice
site together and U2 arrives later by displacing SF1
[@borao2021earlyspliceosome].

What usually gets written as a single 3' splice site is three sequence elements
working together. The branchpoint supplies the acceptor nucleotide for the first
chemical step. The polypyrimidine tract has an operational definition rather
than a motif: an uninterrupted run of pyrimidines, strength counted in uridines,
sitting between the branchpoint and the terminal AG, where U2AF65 binds it.
Recognition of the 3' end can therefore fail without the AG itself being touched
[@borao2021earlyspliceosome].

Neither signal is as fixed as the diagrams suggest. In humans the branchpoint is
barely a consensus, YUNAY, and one of those positions is unconstrained. Budding
yeast holds a near-invariant UACUAAC instead [@borao2021earlyspliceosome]. On
the 5' side only the first two bases of a human intron, GU, are reliably
conserved, and every other position varies. The last three nucleotides of the
upstream exon also affect how tightly U1 binds. Human 5' splice sites therefore
span a broad range of interaction strengths rather than sorting into matches and
mismatches [@borao2021earlyspliceosome].

That degeneracy is the enabling condition for everything else in the book.
Splice site motifs degenerated over evolution in a way that permitted regulated
splicing, and spliceosome complexity increased alongside them. Budding yeast
splices mainly constitutively, humans alternatively
[@borao2021earlyspliceosome]. Constitutive and alternative splicing are two
regimes of one mechanism.

### A second spliceosome, running in parallel

About 0.5 per cent of introns are removed by a different machine entirely.
Roughly 700 human genes carry a U12-type intron, against 19 genes in
*Drosophila*, and a gene that has one usually has exactly one among many
ordinary introns [@akinyi2021minorspliceosome].

The two intron classes are told apart by their signals rather than by their
chemistry. A polypyrimidine tract belongs to major U2-type introns only. The
minor 3' splice site is read by ZRSR2 in place of the U2AF heterodimer. U12
signals are much better conserved, and they support correspondingly less
alternative splicing [@akinyi2021minorspliceosome].

A review of the same system puts the share lower, below 0.4 per cent of all
human introns, and names the machinery that removes them as U11, U12, U4atac, U5
and U6atac [@elmarabti2021minorintron]. Both figures are small, and the
difference between them matters only where a count of minor introns is being
used as a denominator.

## The five event names, and what they leave out {#sec-event-classes}

Most descriptions of alternative splicing use five names: exon skipping,
mutually exclusive exons, intron retention, alternative donor and alternative
acceptor. They were inherited as a traditional vocabulary rather than derived.
The paper that formalised event nomenclature says so, and then points out that
real annotations contain many patterns none of the five describes
[@sammeth2008nomenclature].

Across three human reference annotations the four simple classes fall in the
same rank order. Exon skipping is commonest, then alternative donor, then
alternative acceptor, with intron retention last. Those authors state their
denominator: events with a simple splicing pattern, involving at most two
alternative splice sites, and uncorrelated with a variable transcription start
or polyadenylation site [@sammeth2008nomenclature].

Patterns too complex for any of the five names run from 23.18 per cent of
annotated events in RefSeq to 35.4 per cent in Ensembl
[@sammeth2008nomenclature]. Roughly a quarter to a third of annotated
alternative splicing has no textbook label. Which classes dominate also varies
by lineage, and @sec-class-balance gives the plant and fungal picture.

Mutual exclusivity is rarer than its prominence in the literature suggests.
Mutually exclusive exons make up 12 to 14.5 per cent of the complex event pool
depending on the annotation, behind the skipping of two consecutive exons. The
scarcity is attributed to the more elaborate mechanism mutual exclusivity
requires [@sammeth2008nomenclature].

The mixture also differs inside and outside the reading frame. In RefSeq coding
sequence, exon skipping accounts for 50.9 per cent of local events, against 37.9
per cent in 5' UTRs. Intron retention runs the other way, 2.1 per cent in coding
sequence against 8.4 per cent in 5' UTRs. Those authors read the reversal as
selection against in-frame stop codons [@sammeth2008nomenclature].

One class is different in kind from the other four. An unspliced intron seen in
polyadenylated RNA does not establish that a splicing decision was taken. It is
equally compatible with a finished mRNA, with an intermediate accumulating ahead
of a slow rate-limiting step, and with a transcript deliberately stalled while a
later decision is pending [@jacob2017intronretention]. Intron retention is the
only one of the five whose observation leaves the question open.

## Where isoform differences actually sit {#sec-ends}

Alternative polyadenylation produces isoforms with no splicing difference at
all. Choosing among a gene's several poly(A) sites yields transcripts that
differ in 3' UTR, in terminal exon, or in coding potential
[@huang2026apacancer].

The name covers two consequences that should not be pooled. Tandem 3' UTR choice
within the last exon leaves the protein untouched and changes only which
regulatory elements the transcript carries. A poly(A) site used further
upstream, in an intron, an internal exon or an alternative terminal exon, can
truncate the protein outright [@huang2026apacancer].

Splicing turns out to be the minority explanation for tissue-dependent isoform
differences. Measured across 23 human cell types, alternative splicing accounts
for those differences in at most 35 per cent of genes. For 53 per cent of
tissue-dependent exonic regions there was no evidence, or only weak evidence, of
the region ever being spliced out [@reyes2018altstart].

The share that could plausibly change a protein is smaller again. Only about 15
per cent of tissue-dependent splicing involves exons belonging to principal
isoforms. The rest is concentrated in untranslated exons and in non-coding or
minor transcripts [@reyes2018altstart].

Where coding sequence does vary between isoforms, the variation sits at the ends
rather than in the middle. Coding exons in the variable 5' and 3' regions
produced by alternative initiation and termination carry about four times more
alternative nucleotides than the core coding region, which splicing alone can
diversify [@shabalina2014proteinends]. A treatment of isoform biology that
discussed splicing and nothing else would be describing the smaller half of the
phenomenon.

## Measuring how much an exon is used {#sec-psi}

Percent spliced-in, written PSI or Ψ, is the fraction of a gene's mRNAs that
contain a given exon. It was defined on read densities rather than on raw read
counts: the density of inclusion reads, divided by the sum of the inclusion and
exclusion densities [@wang2008alternative]. The metric asks nothing about full
transcripts, which is why the short-read era settled on it.
@sec-short-read-limit gives the constraint that made that necessary.

A single PSI value also conflates two separate splicing acts, one at each end of
the intron. The intron-centric reformulation splits it into a
5' and a 3' index, one per intron end, so that the choice made at the donor and
the choice made at the acceptor are scored separately
[@pervouchine2013introncentric]. Where the two
indices disagree, a single number reports the average of two decisions that were
never taken together.

## Three questions that are easy to confuse {#sec-dtu}

Three study designs ask three different things of the same data. Differential
gene expression asks whether a gene's total transcriptional output changed.
Differential transcript usage asks whether the composition of its isoform
abundance spectrum changed. Differential transcript expression asks whether an
individual transcript changed [@soneson2016differential]. They are different
null hypotheses rather than different resolutions of one.

![The same two-isoform gene under four outcomes. Only transcript usage
distinguishes a gene that redistributed its output from one that did not, and
only gene-level testing is blind to that case.](../figures/dge-dtu-dte.svg){#fig-dge-dtu-dte width=100%}

Exon-level testing sits close to transcript usage without replacing it.
Differential exon usage and differential transcript usage answer the same
question at gene level. Only transcript usage names which isoforms were used
more and which less. Exon counting additionally has to contend with exons whose
boundaries differ between the isoforms containing them [@baldoni2025dtu].

A gene whose total output never moves can still have reversed which protein it
makes.

## When two transcripts count as the same {#sec-transcript-classes}

Transcript identity has to be settled mechanically, and the unit that makes it
checkable is the intron chain. Two transcripts match at intron-chain level when
every intron has identical coordinates and the counts agree, which implies that
all internal exons match. The definition says nothing about where the transcript
starts and ends. Terminal boundaries are deliberately left outside it
[@pertea2020gffutilities], and @sec-three-axes shows what sits in that gap.

Long-read classification is built on the same comparison. A full splice match
reproduces every splice junction of some reference transcript. An incomplete
splice match reproduces a consecutive run of them but not all. Neither category
says the ends agree, which is why an incomplete match can be a genuinely shorter
isoform or a truncated cDNA [@tardaguila2018sqanti].

The novel categories are graded by how far a transcript departs from the
annotation's inventory of splice sites. Novel in catalog uses only annotated
donors and acceptors, either recombined into new junction combinations or newly
paired with each other. Novel not in catalog introduces a donor or acceptor the
annotation does not contain [@tardaguila2018sqanti].

Which comparison was run determines every novelty count in this book. The
reasons published novel-isoform percentages range from a few per cent to more
than half, sometimes for the same data, are worked through in
[the transcript comparison walkthrough](../walkthroughs/intron-chain-comparison.qmd).

## Splicing into decay {#sec-as-nmd}

Whether a stop codon counts as premature is decided by position. A stop at least
50 nucleotides upstream of the last exon junction leaves an exon junction
complex downstream of it after the first round of translation, and that complex
is what triggers decay. The rule was established with reporter constructs rather
than by survey [@lindeboom2016nmdrules].

That makes decay available as a regulatory output. AS-NMD, also published under
the name regulated unproductive splicing and translation, is the proposal that
cells splice deliberately into decay. An isoform is made in order to be
destroyed, so that the fraction of transcripts reaching protein is set after
transcription [@garciamoreno2020asnmd]. On that reading an unproductive isoform
is a product of regulation.

How much of the transcriptome this accounts for depends on a denominator, which
the survey states. With decay inhibited in HeLa cells, high-confidence targets
came to 2,793 isoforms from 2,116 genes. That is 19 per cent of expressed
protein-coding genes. It is also 22 per cent of the 9,440 genes those authors
counted as alternatively spliced, where alternatively spliced means producing
two or more expressed isoforms, including the decay targets themselves
[@french2020asnmdsurvey].

The amount of protein a gene makes is therefore set partly by isoforms that
never become protein.

## How many isoforms does a gene have {#sec-scale}

The answer depends entirely on which genes are counted. Across all Ensembl gene
bodies the median is one isoform. For protein-coding genes the median is six,
the 75th percentile is eleven, and only 14.6 per cent are left with a single
annotated transcript [@page2025annotations].

Annotation and observation part company at the top of that distribution. Ensembl
lists 7,255 genes with ten or more isoforms, 256 with fifty or more, and 30 with
a hundred or more. The same authors quantified nine GTEx tissues with long reads
and observed at most 105 isoforms for any gene body, and 60 for any
protein-coding gene, while accepting a single uniquely aligned read as evidence
[@page2025isoformdiversity].

Dominance needs defining before it can be counted, and the phrase hides two
claims. The major transcript is whichever has the highest expression within a
gene. A dominant transcript is a major transcript expressed at considerably more
than any minor one, operationalised as at least twice the abundance of the next.
That held for almost 80 per cent of expressed genes in primary tissues
[@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript].

Expression is sparser than annotation in the ordinary case. In primary tissues
the ratio of expressed transcripts to genes averaged 1.12, just over one
transcript per gene [@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript]. What survives of the
functional claim, once that is taken into account, is the subject of
@sec-how-functional.

The median protein-coding gene in one Ensembl release carries annotation for
six isoforms, and a separate short-read study of primary tissues put the ratio
of expressed transcripts to genes at about one. The two were not measured on
the same footing, so the distance between them is not a measured gap.
@sec-per-gene-counts returns to the question once the catalogues are in view.
